The Poison:
The article monetizes voter frustration to sell commercial services, masking a marketing pitch as news.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The Plane Error is Q1 (Who). The article claims to serve the public interest (voter sentiment) but actually serves the commercial interest of the pollster.

Social Physics Analysis:
NumberBarn uses a 'Smart Selfish' loop. They identify a common annoyance (political texts), amplify it via a 'poll,' and project the solution as their own service. It's a manufactured crisis for commercial extraction.

The Trajectory: The Path of Awakening into Destruction.
The claim of public service masks a commercial extraction. Modal Dynamics: will be -> is not via Red Top (The Imperial Trap).

The Unavoidable Truth: Political spam is genuinely annoying to most voters.
The Unavoidable Lie: This poll is an objective, neutral analysis of voter sentiment rather than a marketing asset.

The article conflates commercial PR with public discourse. It exploits genuine annoyance to sell a product, eroding trust in both news and civic engagement.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Americans fed up with all the constant campaign texting — and it could backfire on candidates: poll

With midterm elections just nine days away, Americans are fed up with getting blitzed with constant campaign calls and text messages and warned that candidates who overdo it could get punished at the ballot box, a new poll claims.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Ping!

Americans are fed up with getting blitzed with constant campaign calls and text messages, a new poll found — as voters warned they might punish candidates who overdo it at the ballot box.

A new nationwide survey from phone number management company NumberBarn found that Americans report receiving an average of 13 political calls and texts per week as campaigns ramp up their voter contact ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3.

Six in 10 respondents said the campaign messages are “excessive” compared with past elections.

The survey found:

“Trust may be one of the biggest challenges facing political outreach,” the NumberBarn analysis of the findings said.

“Nearly 8 in 10 Americans (79%) say they do not trust the accuracy of the information they receive through political calls and texts. Political calls and texts are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but the findings suggest that more messages do not necessarily mean more influence, trust, or engagement.”

Americans who’ve had enough have taken drastic measures to stop the text-and-call blitz.

More than one-in-four Americans (26%) said they pay a one-time fee to permanently block campaign calls and texts and 57% stopped taking calls from unknown numbers.

In addition, 23% of respondents turn on a “silence unknown callers” setting and 10% turn their phone off or used the “Do Not Disturb” setting during peak election season, while 3% said they changed their phone number.

More than half (51%) of Americans said political texts should only be sent to people who opted in first. Another 20% say campaigns should send far fewer messages.

“As Americans grow accustomed to screening unknown numbers, blocking spam texts, and questioning the origin of every message — whether it’s a candidate, a scammer, or AI — reaching a voter’s phone is getting easier, but winning their attention remains the real battle,” the poll analysis said.

In September 2026, NumberBarn surveyed 1,006 U.S. adults to gauge how Americans view political calls, text messages, and other election-related communication ahead of the 2026 midterm election. It has a margin of error plus or minus percentage points.

NumberBarn is a telecommunications service provider specializing in phone number management, including purchasing, parking, transferring and forwarding phone numbers.
